claim: Imitation Dunsany is diagnosed as elaborate made-up names, vague gorgeous cities and many sentences beginning with 'And' — biblical cadence worn as costume.
source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
quote: a great many sentences beginning with "And."

verdict.trueWording: a lot of elaborate made-up names, some vague descriptions of gorgeous cities and unmentionable dooms, and a great many sentences beginning with "And."
verdict.note: p.5 quotation is verbatim and the three diagnostic items are exactly on the page. The essay names the King James Bible only as a formative influence on Dunsany's OWN prose ('one of the profoundest formative influences on Dunsany's prose'; imitators are out of reach unless 'brought up from the cradle on the grand sonorities of Genesis and Ecclesiastes'); it never attributes the imitators' 'And' sentences to biblical cadence, and never frames them as costume. That reading is a defensible inference, not the page's statement.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: biblical cadence worn as costume -- the essay ties the KJV to Dunsany himself, never says imitators wear biblical cadence as costume

claim: Mike Cadden characterizes the Earthsea narration as free indirect discourse in which the protagonist's feelings blend with the narrator's, creating sympathy while keeping narrative flexibility.
source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Cadden, Beyond Genre)

verdict.trueWording: makes the narrator seem sympathetic, does not distance his thoughts
verdict.note: Raw wikitext: 'This narrative technique, which Cadden characterizes as "free indirect discourse", makes the narrator of the book seem sympathetic to the protagonist, and does not distance his thoughts from the reader.' Quote verbatim; 'Mike Cadden' confirmed elsewhere on the same page ('Scholar Mike Cadden'); sympathy limb supported; blending of protagonist feelings with narration supported only loosely ('does not distance his thoughts from the reader') and stated squarely on the SEPARATE Ursula K. Le Guin article, not this one. Nothing on this page says anything about narrative flexibility.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'while keeping narrative flexibility' - the cited page never claims the technique preserves flexibility

claim: Slusser (1976) called the Earthsea cycle a work of high style and imagination with genuine epic vision.
source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Slusser)
quote: work of high style and imagination

verdict.trueWording: Slusser: "work of high style and imagination"; "genuine epic vision" cited to Cadden
verdict.note: Raw wikitext: 'Slusser described the Earthsea cycle as a "work of high style and imagination",{{sfn|Slusser|1976|pp=32-35}} and the original trilogy of books a product of "genuine epic vision".{{sfn|Cadden|2005|p=86}}' The quoted limb is verbatim and is Slusser 1976. The second limb is footnoted to Cadden 2005 and its object is the original trilogy, not the cycle.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'the Earthsea cycle ... with genuine epic vision' per Slusser 1976 - the page applies 'genuine epic vision' to the original trilogy and footnotes it to Cadden 2005

claim: The NEA Big Read web page repeats the guide's 'plain, strong, and exact' characterization and pairs it with Craig's 'taut and clean as a ship's sail'.
source: NEA Big Read: A Wizard of Earthsea (web page)

verdict.trueWording: Page credits 'taut and clean' to The Guardian, unnamed
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the attribution of 'taut and clean as a ship's sail' to Craig - the page credits that quotation only to 'The Guardian' and the string 'Craig' does not occur anywhere in the page's HTML (case-insensitive grep of the raw source returned zero hits)
verdict.note: Live arts.gov page fetched (HTTP 200, 74,952 bytes). Both quotations ARE on the page: the Overview carries '...it is written in prose as taut and clean as a ship's sail.... It poses the deep questions about life, death, power and responsibility that children need answering' (The Guardian), and an accordion panel reproduces the guide's 'Language of Fantasy' text verbatim including 'plain, strong, and exact'. So the 'repeats the guide's characterization' limb and the 'pairs it with' limb are both supported; only the Craig attribution is absent from the page. (Amanda Craig did write the Guardian review, but that cannot be verified from this URL, which is what was cited.)

claim: Searoad's nonfantastic stories convey 'the same capably restrained immanence' — restraint named as a constant of her manner.
source: Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (SFE), entry 'Le Guin, Ursula K'

verdict.trueWording: conveys some of the same capably restrained immanence
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim on the raw page, of Searoad's nonfantastic Oregon-coast stories: 'Searoad: The Chronicles of Klatsand (coll 1991), assembling nonfantastic stories set on the Oregon coast, conveys some of the same capably restrained immanence.' But the page hedges ('some of the same') and applies it only backward to the Orsinia nonfantastic work; 'restrained' occurs exactly once in the whole entry (grep: 1 hit), so restraint is never named as a constant of her manner.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: restraint named as a constant of her manner — the page says only 'some of the same' immanence, of the Orsinian nonfantastic work

claim: Attebery (quoted by Garth) distinguishes her from Tolkien copyists as one who absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him and went her own direction.
quote: absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him, and gone on in her own direction

verdict.trueWording: absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him, and gone on in her own direction
verdict.note: Quotation is on the page word for word and Attebery (The Fantasy Tradition in American Literature) does distinguish Le Guin from 'the Tolkien copyists' — but it is NOT Garth's text: it appears in a reader comment by David Bratman (28 Jan 2021), to which Garth replied 'Absolutely spot on!'. Attribution limb fails.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'quoted by Garth' — the Attebery quotation appears in a reader comment by David Bratman, not in Garth's post

claim: Garth notes Le Guin called language invention 'the Secret Vice' after Tolkien's essay and counted LOTR among the three books she had re-read past counting.

verdict.trueWording: lost count only with Dickens, Tolstoy, and Tolkien
verdict.note: Secret Vice limb fully supported: 'In Always Coming Home (1985), Le Guin refers to language invention as "what an illustrious predecessor referred to as the Secret Vice" ... She meant Tolkien, whose essay "A Secret Vice"'. But the re-reading limb is misstated: Garth quotes her on LOTR — 'I reread a great deal, but have lost count only with Dickens, Tolstoy, and Tolkien' — three AUTHORS, not three books.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'the three books she had re-read past counting' — the page names three authors (Dickens, Tolstoy, Tolkien), not three books

claim: Tearle credits Le Guin with picking up the right word on the end of her pen; Plotz devotes a chapter to her use of language and naming and to the careful, deliberate nature of her prose.
source: Oliver Tearle, review of Plotz (Interesting Literature)
quote: the careful and deliberate nature of her prose

verdict.trueWording: Plotz discusses her prose's care; the chapter covers language and naming.
verdict.note: Both quoted phrases are verbatim: 'the right word on the end of her pen' (Tearle, borrowing Chesterton on Stevenson) and 'the careful and deliberate nature of her prose'. But the latter sits in a separate sentence about Plotz's discussion generally ('He is persuasive when discussing Le Guin's style, the careful and deliberate nature of her prose, and the way she creates an alien world through ingenious use of language'), not in the chapter list, which reads: 'a chapter on the \u2018simple joy\u2019 of reading Le Guin's work, especially her use of language and the power of naming'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the chapter (as opposed to the book generally) is devoted to the careful, deliberate nature of her prose

claim: She scans a chapter closely, hears its close 'like drumbeats', and recommends reading passages aloud.
source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)

verdict.trueWording: She reads the lines aloud herself; no recommendation appears on the page.
verdict.note: 'like drumbeats' is verbatim ('They are like drumbeats.') and the close reading of chapter 8 of Fellowship, 'Fog on the Barrow Downs', is on the page. But the page's only read-aloud sentence is Le Guin's own practice: 'Reading the lines aloud I can't help thinking of a Beethoven finale'. The two occurrences of 'recommend' on the page are Nepveu's (a friend recommending the essay; asking for further recommendations), not Le Guin recommending reading aloud.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that she recommends reading passages aloud \u2014 the page shows her reading them aloud, not advising it

claim: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next; pace and movement depend on rhythm you can only control by hearing it.
source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)
quote: duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next

verdict.trueWording: the primary way you feel and control rhythm is by hearing it.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim: 'The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence\u2014to keep the story going.' Page then says 'Pace and movement depend above all on rhythm, and the primary way you feel and control the rhythm of your prose is by hearing it\u2014by listening to it.' The claim hardens 'the primary way' into an exclusive 'only'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that rhythm can ONLY be controlled by hearing it \u2014 the page says hearing is the primary way, not the sole one

feature: scholarly focus: voice and rhythm, not lexis
claim: Weyant's secondary bibliography shows the style-adjacent scholarship clusters on narrative voice and structure (Adams 1991; Jose 1991; Castleman 2020), rhythm (Barry & Prescott 1992), and the 'language of realism' in terrain (Pegg 1995) — no stylometric or corpus study is listed.
source: Curtis Weyant, The Left Hand of Darkness: Secondary Bibliography

verdict.trueWording: Bary, Nora. 'Beyond Words: The Impact of Rhythm as Narrative Technique...' Extrapolation 33 (1992): 154-65
verdict.unsupportedLimb: '(Barry & Prescott 1992)' as what Weyant's bibliography shows - the page lists that rhythm article under 'Bary, Nora' alone: the surname is misspelled and co-author Mary Prescott is not named there (Crossref, checked at index 95, confirms Barry & Prescott is the true attribution, but this page does not show it)
verdict.note: curtisweyant.com fetched live (200, 253 KB HTML -> 30 KB text; list runs A-W in both the scholarly and the blog sections, so it is complete, not lazy-loaded). Confirmed on the page: Adams, Rebecca, 'Narrative Voice and Unimaginability of the Utopian Feminine...', Utopian Studies 2.1-2 (1991): 35-47; Jose, Jim, 'Reflections on the Politics of Le Guin's Narrative Shifts', SFS 18.2 (1991): 180-97; Castleman, Samantha, 'Narrative Organization as Cultural Training in the Left Hand of Darkness', Femspec 19.2 (2020): 10-24; Pegg, Barry, 'Down to Earth: Terrain, Territory, and the Language of Realism...', Michigan Academician 27 (1995): 481-92 ('Language of Realism' verbatim). The negative limb also holds: case-insensitive search of the whole page returns 0 hits for 'styl' (so no style/stylistic/stylometry), 0 for 'corpus', 0 for 'quantitative', 0 for 'diction', 0 for 'prose'.

claim: Le Guin prescribes the opening chapter of The Return of the Native, a landscape description in which nothing happens, as the cure for that fear.
source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy' (Los Angeles Times, 5 Jan 2003), on ursulakleguin.com
quote: a description of a landscape, in which absolutely nothing happens
page: parenthesis in the 'show don't tell' paragraph
routeHint: direct fetch, HTML stripped to text

verdict.trueWording: landscape description where nothing happens until a man appears
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim on the raw page and the prescription limb holds ('I make them read the first chapter of The Return of the Native'; 'If that won't cure them nothing will'). But the source sentence continues past the quoted cut: '...in which absolutely nothing happens UNTIL IN THE LAST PARAGRAPH A MAN IS SEEN, from far away, walking along a road.' The claim's unqualified 'in which nothing happens' drops that, and the quote as recorded is a mid-sentence truncation that must not be reused without the continuation or an ellipsis.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the claim's 'in which nothing happens' — the page says nothing happens *until in the last paragraph a man is seen walking along a road*

claim: The 1989 revised Women's Press text quoted by Carey reads 'the careless reader's even noticing' where the 1973 Pendragon text reads 'the careless readers even noticing'.
source: Stan Carey quoting the 1989 revised edition of 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie', Sentence first
quote: without the careless reader's even noticing
routeHint: direct fetch; compared against the 1973 Pendragon PDF read in this sweep

verdict.trueWording: without the careless reader's even noticing
verdict.note: The quotation is verbatim on the page, and Carey's copy is identified as the revised 1989 Women's Press edition. But the page never mentions a Pendragon edition, a 1973 text, or any variant reading: 'Pendragon' appears zero times and the only 1973 dates are essay composition dates. The edition-comparison is the verifier's, not the source's.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the 1973 Pendragon text's reading 'the careless readers even noticing' - no variant, no Pendragon edition, and no textual comparison appears on the page
